data.caption: bodyskinjournal.com
data.copy:
japan's drainage canals are so clean they have fish living in them and the reason behind it is bigger than you think

Japan is arguably the cleanest country on earth. And it's not close.

Their toilets have heated seats, automatic bidets, deodorizing filters, and sound machines to mask noise. Their bullet trains get fully cleaned in exactly 7 minutes between stops, with the cleaning teams bowing to passengers on the way out. Their kids scrub their own classrooms for 15 minutes at the end of every school day starting at age 6, because Japan doesn't hire janitors. Their homes have separate slippers for the toilet room so nothing from that room ever touches the rest of the house. And their World Cup fans famously stay after every match to clean the entire stadium themselves, section by section, using 3,000 blue trash bags they bring with them.

Underneath every one of those habits is a Shinto belief that every object has a spirit and every spirit deserves respect. A toilet. A train seat. A body. If you use something, you clean it. If you touch something, you leave it better than you found it. That's not a marketing slogan. That's a thousand-year-old cultural law.

Which means when Japan approaches body hygiene, they don't play. A Japanese shower takes 15 to 20 minutes minimum. Every inch of the body gets a real, deep, deliberate scrub-down. Every single day. There's a Japanese word for what comes off during this process — aka. It's the visible layer of dead skin, oil, and daily grime that lifts when there's real friction pulling against it. The entire ritual is called aka-suri. Literally, "removal of dead skin." Kids are taught aka-suri the same way they're taught to eat with chopsticks.

And so the average Japanese adult can visually see the difference between being clean and being wet with soap. Most Americans cannot. It's not a personal failing. Nobody was ever taught the difference here.

And then there's how you're showering.

data.copy:
Whatever you do, don't swallow another garlic, beetroot, or cayenne pepper capsule from those Facebook brands until you've seen the heavy metals report. Spoiler: most of them don't have one.

I know. The ads are everywhere. Slick packaging. Bold promises. Cardiovascular this. Nitric oxide that. $30 a bottle if you buy three.

Here's what those ads don't tell you. Beetroot, garlic, cayenne, turmeric, ashwagandha — all the botanicals trending in your feed right now — are notorious for absorbing lead, arsenic, and cadmium from contaminated soil. The same property that makes them "natural" makes them magnets for everything in the dirt they grew in. The only thing standing between you and slow toxic accumulation in your kidneys, liver, and bones is a third-party heavy metal test on every batch.

Most Facebook brands skip the test entirely. The certificate of analysis is "available on request" — which means it doesn't exist. Some publish one COA from a 2022 batch and quietly let it lapse for every lot since.

Now pick up the bottle next time you order. Check the back. You'll usually find three more things missing.

No barcode. No manufacturing date. No batch number.

That's not an accident. That's how unregulated supplement brands ship product fast, cheap, and untraceable. Every legitimate manufacturer is required to assign each lot a manufacturing date, a unique batch number, and a scannable barcode tied to a verifiable supply chain. It's the bare minimum. Most of the brands flooding your feed don't even meet that bar.

A barcode is the difference between a real supply chain and a bedroom packing operation. A manufacturing date is the difference between actives that work and a softgel that's been sitting in a warehouse for two years. A heavy metal test is the difference between a vascular supplement and a daily dose of contamination.

adstatus.allowed_values: active (lastSeen or updated_at within last 4 days), inactive (neither field within last 4 days), All/empty (no status filter).
adstatus.notes: find_winning_products forces active. Same as dashboard Status = Active.

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.
